Shares of the nuclear energy start-up crashed in the last quarter of 2025 and continued their downward slide into 2026, losing 29.2% value in the first half of the year, according to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence . President Donald Trump aims to quadruple U.S. nuclear energy capacity to 400 gigawatts by 2050. Because building a traditional nuclear reactor takes years even as power demand has hit unprecedented levels amid the artificial intelligence (AI) data center boom, the government is also supporting small modular reactors (SMRs). Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » NuScale's SMR design is already approved by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and the company has begun manufacturing its first patented 77-megawatt carbon-free modules. The problem? NuScale hasn't built a reactor yet. As that reality set in, investors ran for the exit. Here is how the fallout unfolded. Image source: Getty Images. Whu NuScale Power stock derailed In early 2026, TD Cowen analyst Marc Bianchi raised alarm bells, warning that NuScale's flagship project in Romania could be delayed until 2034. NuScale's fourth-quarter earnings report delivered another blow: a massive $507.4 million milestone payment to ENTRA1 Energy, its exclusive commercialization partner. Under the agreement, NuScale owes ENTRA1 fees for its nuclear product developments without guaranteed revenues. With the company's operating loss surging nearly fivefold to $690 million during the quarter, analysts slashed their price targets on NuScale stock while some disgruntled investors filed class action lawsuits, alleging misrepresentation of ENTRA1 Energy's capabilities and arrangement. To make matters worse, NuScale's largest shareholder, Fluor , aggressively offloaded its position and exited NuScale completely by April 2026, pocketing $2.4 billion in proceeds. Watching an anchor insider walk away shattered whatever little remained of retail confidence. NuScale's first quarter offered no relief. Revenue plummeted from $13.4 million in the prior-year period to a paltry $0.5 million as one-time licensing revenue dried up, while net losses nearly tripled to $44 million. Story Continues Is NuScalePower stock a buy before Aug. 5? NuScale did finish Q1 with $890 million in cash and short-term investments and zero long-term debt. But cash reserves can only buy so much time when losses are mounting, and cash burn rates remain high. Commercial deployment is still years away, with NuScale projecting first module delivery no earlier than 2031. Moreover, although ENTRA1 has been in the headlines for a big agreement with the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) to deploy up to 6 GW of nuclear power with NuScale's SMR equipment, the project still lacks a long-term power purchase agreement or a finalized timeline. NuScale will release its second-quarter numbers on Aug. 5. Expectations are muted. Until the company can transition from regulatory approvals and partnership agreements to a firm revenue-generating model, its stock will remain speculative and volatile. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo in Milan, Italy. The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo in Milan, Italy. The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Italy Milan luxury shops close as Italy prepares to deploy troops in the city after days of protests Demonstrations over poor public services and rising costs spiralled over the weekend, with shops looted and property vandalised Why are people protesting across Europe? Reuters Mon 19 Oct 2026 20.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Italy’s government will dispatch 500 army troops to “defend Milan” after two days ⁠of unrest that saw demonstrators ⁠clash with police, ​loot shops and vandalise property, deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday. The deployment is expected to be included in a package of security measures to be approved at ⁠a cabinet meeting expected on Tuesday, and comes as shops in central Milan closed early and boarded up their windows, fearing a fresh outbreak of violence in Italy’s financial capital. Why are people protesting across Europe? Read more “From words to action: 500 more ⁠troops to defend Milan,” Salvini, head of the co-ruling right-wing League party, wrote on social media. Most stores in Milan’s Via ​Montenapoleone luxury shopping district, home to brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior, had removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution, while police patrolled the street and a handful of tourists looked on. Several hundred hooded ‌protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze and looted shops in the city centre over the weekend after an initially peaceful demonstration on Saturday over poor public services and rising costs. View image in fullscreen In Galleria Vittorio Emanuele, some shops are closed and have been cleared of their merchandise, others have their display windows covered and security increased. Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/Shutterstock Among the stores ransacked were sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed. Clothing brands Levi’s and Under Armour, as well as Decathlon, covered their shop windows with cardboard and wooden panels. Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who ‌faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs on Monday to discuss the situation. “The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X. As part of the planned crackdown, the Corriere della Sera newspaper said Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, while bringing forward some provisions contained in an existing security bill currently being examined by parliament. View image in fullscreen Damage to a Decathlon store in Milan following clashes between protesters and police. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Italian ⁠police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of ​those taken to police stations, 32 were ​arrested, including 23 minors and 13 ​foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities. The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday. The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France , where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years. https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: Overnight, a handful of Republicans have spoken out against Donald Trump’s softening stance on Russia, threatening to pull financial support for his agenda over his “embarrassing” handling of the Ukraine war. Don Bacon, an outgoing congressman in Nebraska, condemned Trump’s actions – which include a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel and the pausing of sanctions on Moscow – as “absolutely disgraceful” and accused the US president of cozying up to a “war criminal” in Vladimir Putin, his Russian counterpart. “It really is disgraceful, and the Republicans that I associate with, there’s a lot of us, can’t stand it,” Bacon told CNN on Monday. “I think the president’s leverage in this Congress is shot.” Last week, Trump waived sanctions imposed on Russia through a law named after his longtime ally and late senator Lindsey Graham. The legislation, which he signed only last month, was intended to increase financial pressure on Russia, more than four years after it invaded Ukraine. Instea

https://www.baltictimes.com/balance_must.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Balance must be found between interests of Latvia’s film industry and cooperation with U.S. regarding streaming fees - president 2026-10-07 LETA/TBT Staff RIGA - On the issue of streaming fees, the interests of the Latvian film industry must be balanced with cooperation with the U.S., President Edgars Rinkevics told reporters after meeting with Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) on Wednesday. The president noted that he understands the industry’s concerns about not introducing the fee and seeking other solutions. He said that work on the relevant bill will continue in the Saeima and that the interests and funding of the film industry must be balanced with cooperation with the U.S. The implementation of European Union requirements is also essential. The president also referred to his visit to the U.S., which he described as successful, noting the attraction of film companies and the promotion of economic cooperation. Rinkevics emphasized that the Prime Minister and the relevant ministries will work on a solution. In his view, a solution will be reached that will satisfy industry representatives while maintaining good relations with strategic partners. The president concluded that this will take some time and may require additional work. Prime Minister Kulbergs, for his part, stated that it is not worth jeopardizing relations with Latvia’s strategic partner, the United States, over EUR 600,000. He said that if this issue is particularly important to the partner, the EUR 600,000 for the film industry will be found and secured, thereby not losing economic opportunities in cooperation with the U.S. The prime minister noted that he personally enjoys Latvian national films and that he has always advocated for domestic cinema, and that this has not changed this time either. In Kulbergs’ view, the industry’s reaction is based on a misunderstanding, as this is not about taking action against the film industry. Speaking about economic opportunities, Kulbergs referred to the meeting between the President and the Latvian Ambassador to the U.S. with 300 top-level business representatives and emphasized the strengthening of Latvia’s economic ties with the U.S. The Prime Minister noted that if there is a desire for an ally to support Latvia’s security and station its contingent here, there should be no dispute over the issue of fees, especially since the cooperation offers other, far greater benefits. He promised to resolve the issue with the film industry. As previously reported, the Saeima’s human rights and public affairs committee endorsed amendments at the end of September for a final reading, which require audiovisual service providers to invest at least 3.5 percent of their revenue generated in Latvia annually in the production of local audiovisual content. The aim of the regulation is to promote the production of Latvian films and TV series and to ensure wider availability of local content on streaming platforms. It was also reported that Kulbergs stated on Monday that the government should consider abandoning the proposed tax on streaming platforms and instead focus more on supporting the development of the film industry. The Latvian Film Producers Association, the Latvian Cinematographers Union, and the Latvian Film Directors Guild had expressed confusion regarding Kulbergs’ statement.
